config.title: Default Props

intro.title: Default Props
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that displays a greeting message. You will learn how to use default props to provide fallback values for component properties when they are not explicitly passed. The core concepts involve defining a component with TypeScript interfaces and using the `defaultProps` static property. This will help you create more robust and user-friendly components in React with TypeScript.
intro.usecase: Default props are essential for building reusable React components that need to work reliably even when some data is missing. For example, in a dashboard, a chart component might use default props to display placeholder data or a neutral color scheme if the user hasn't yet selected a dataset. Similarly, form input components often have default placeholder text or validation rules to ensure they render correctly before any user interaction. This pattern prevents UI errors and provides a consistent baseline experience across applications like e-commerce filters, data tables, and modal dialogs.

objectives: Initialize default values for component props using TypeScript interfaces
Configure React components to render with fallback prop values when none are provided
Apply default props to functional components using ES6 destructuring syntax
Construct TypeScript interfaces that define both required and optional props with defaults
Update existing components to include default prop configurations
Manipulate prop values to demonstrate priority when defaults are overridden by parent components
Integrate default props with conditional rendering logic in component implementations

steps.title: Import React and TypeScript utilities
steps.instruction: Import React and the FC (FunctionComponent) type from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React and FC into your file. FC is a TypeScript utility type for defining functional components.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a type from a library
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: Your file will have the necessary imports to create a typed functional component.
successCriteria: React and FC are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and the FC type from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to import React and the FC type from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Define the component props interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named GreetingProps with two properties: a required string property 'name' and an optional string property 'greeting'.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions inside curly braces.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and FC here

// Define the GreetingProps interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface named GreetingProps with the specified properties will be created.
successCriteria: GreetingProps interface exists with required 'name' (string) and optional 'greeting' (string) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your interface has both the required 'name' property and optional 'greeting' property with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match the requirements. Please define an interface named GreetingProps with a required string 'name' and an optional string 'greeting'.

steps.title: Create Greeting with React.FC<GreetingProps>
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Greeting annotated as React.FC<GreetingProps>. Return a simple <h1> with the text 'Hello, World!'. You may use a parameterless arrow function (() => { ... }) here; using the props in JSX comes in a later step.
steps.hint: Use the GreetingProps interface you defined earlier as the generic on React.FC (e.g. React.FC<GreetingProps>). Return the required <h1> JSX; an empty parameter list () => is fine here.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a Greeting component typed with React.FC<GreetingProps> that renders an <h1> with 'Hello, World!'.
successCriteria: The Greeting component is defined using React.FC<GreetingProps> and returns an <h1> element with the text 'Hello, World!'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using React.FC<GreetingProps> and returning the correct JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you're using the correct type and returning JSX.

steps.title: Add component implementation without default props
steps.instruction: Inside the Greeting component, implement the JSX to display the name and message props directly without any default values.
steps.hint: Return JSX that uses the props passed to the component. For example, you could display them in a heading and paragraph.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Greeting component will render the provided name and message props in the UI when used.
successCriteria: The JSX displays the name prop
The JSX displays the message prop
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying both the name and message props in your JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try implementing the component to return JSX that displays the name and message props.

steps.title: Use the component with all required props
steps.instruction: Add the Greeting component to your app's return statement, passing both required props: name and message.
steps.hint: Use the Greeting component like a regular JSX element, providing both props as attributes.
steps.analogousExample:
// Using a component with required props
<Button label="Click me" onClick={handleClick} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The Greeting component will be rendered with the provided name and message values.
successCriteria: The Greeting component is included in the App's return statement with both name and message props specified.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the Greeting component, but make sure you're providing both the name and message props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Greeting component isn't being used correctly. Add it to the App's return statement with both required props.

steps.title: Attempt to use component with missing optional props
steps.instruction: Add a second Greeting component inside the App component's return statement, but this time omit the message prop entirely. After you fix defaults in later steps, this same second line will demonstrate the default message—no need to add another Greeting again.
steps.hint: Add another <Greeting /> below the first, with only the name prop (e.g. <Greeting name="Bob" />). The Output tab often mounts the first top-level const (Greeting) in isolation, so comparing two instances is mainly visible in your App JSX here.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see a TypeScript error because the message prop is required but not provided.
successCriteria: A second Greeting component is added with only the name prop, intentionally omitting the required message prop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a second component, but it might still have all required props. Try removing the message prop entirely to see the TypeScript error.
steps.feedbackWrong: Make sure you add a second Greeting component inside the App's return statement, but only provide the name prop without the message prop.

steps.title: Define default props using destructuring with defaults
steps.instruction: Modify the Greeting component to use destructuring with default values for the message prop. Set the default message to 'Welcome!'
steps.hint: In the function parameters, add a default value after the destructured prop: ({ name, message = 'Welcome!' })
steps.expectedOutcome: The Greeting component now has a default value for the message prop, so it can be used without explicitly providing a message.
successCriteria: The Greeting component's destructuring includes a default value for the message prop set to 'Welcome!'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've added the default value correctly in the destructuring. It should look like: message = 'Welcome!'
steps.feedbackWrong: modify the Greeting component's function parameters to include a default value for the message prop.

steps.title: Create a defaultProps object
steps.instruction: Add a defaultProps static property to the Greeting component, setting message to 'Welcome!'.
steps.hint: In TypeScript with React.FC, you can assign defaultProps directly to the component after its definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Greeting component will have a defaultProps property that provides a default value for the message prop.
successCriteria: Greeting.defaultProps is defined with message set to 'Welcome!'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that defaultProps is assigned correctly to Greeting with the message property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The defaultProps property wasn't added correctly. Make sure to assign an object with message: 'Welcome!' to Greeting.defaultProps.

steps.title: Compare both default props approaches
steps.instruction: Add a comment below the Greeting component that explains the difference between destructuring defaults and defaultProps, and when you might choose each approach.
steps.hint: Write a comment that starts with // and describes the two approaches. Mention that destructuring defaults work at runtime and defaultProps is a static property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Destructuring defaults are applied when the component function runs.
// defaultProps is a static property that TypeScript can read for type checking.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a comment that explains the two ways to set default props in React with TypeScript.
successCriteria: A comment is added that mentions both destructuring defaults and defaultProps, and includes a brief note about when to use each.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but it doesn't fully explain both approaches or when to use them. Make sure to mention destructuring defaults and defaultProps, and give a reason for choosing one over the other.
steps.feedbackWrong: No comment was added, or the comment doesn't discuss default props approaches. Please add a comment that explains the difference between destructuring defaults and defaultProps.
